pages.title: ROAS is not profit: how we report paid ads

items.text: ROAS is not profit: how we report paid ads
A 6× return can still lose money. Here is the number we report instead.
Return on ad spend is the number everyone quotes, and it can look great while a business loses money.
A 6× ROAS on a product with a 15% margin still loses money once you count shipping, returns and the cost of the creative. ROAS also ignores customers who would have bought anyway.
Contribution after ad spend: revenue minus product costs, shipping and ads
New-customer cost: what it costs to win someone who never bought before
Payback period: how many days until a new customer has paid for their ad
We would rather show you a smaller number that is true than a bigger one that isn't.
Budgets move to the campaigns that make money, not the ones that look good in a screenshot.

Reviews, pages and links: the three things that still decide who shows up first near you.

Volume, freshness and replies. A steady five reviews a month beats fifty in one week, and every reply is a small signal that someone is home.
One page per service and per area you actually serve, written for people, with real photos and real prices.

Opening hours kept current, including holidays
Photos from the real location, updated monthly
Local links count more than big ones: the chamber of commerce, a nearby school, the paper that covered your opening.

pages.title: Agency or in-house? An honest comparison

items.text: Agency or in-house? An honest comparison
What it really costs to hire a marketing team, and when an agency makes more sense.
It depends on three numbers: what you can spend a year, how many channels you need, and how fast you need results.
A senior SEO lead, a social producer and a paid ads specialist cost well over $300k a year in New York before tools, software and management time. That buys three people, each covering one channel.
Tools: rank tracking, ad software, editing, scheduling
The months it takes before a new team ships anything
For a fraction of that you get a team that already works together, already owns the tools and has seen what works in other accounts this month.
Hire in-house when marketing is the product. Hire an agency when it has to work next quarter.
Most of our clients use both: one marketer in-house who owns the brand, and us for the channels that need specialists.
